title: Love, described
text: Love is patient and is kind; love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
body: Read at weddings, written to a church tearing itself apart. Paul is not being romantic; he is describing behaviour to people who had stopped behaving.

Every item is a verb or a refusal — things you do, or decline to do, on a Tuesday. Not one of them is a feeling. That is the mercy of the passage: love of this kind is available to you on a day you do not feel it.
Takes no account of evil is a bookkeeping term. It means refusing to keep the ledger of what was said, and how often, and who started it.
question: Which line of that list would the person closest to you say you fail?
practice: Read the list slowly with one person in mind. Pick one item and do it today.
prayer: God, I want to feel love. Teach me to do it on the days I do not.

title: What comes out of your mouth
text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
body: The word for corrupt is what you would say about rotten fruit. Paul's category is not rude words but words that decay the person who hears them.
The standard he sets is high enough to be uncomfortable: speech should build, according to the need — theirs, not your need to say it.
That single test defuses most arguments. Not is it true, but does saying it now build. Plenty of true things fail that test.
question: What do you say to the people at home that you would never say to a colleague?
practice: Before your next hard conversation, ask: does this build, and is now the need?
prayer: Lord, guard my mouth at home the way I guard it at work.

title: Before the sun goes down
text: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
body: Anger itself is permitted. Paul quotes a psalm to say so, which should settle the idea that a good Christian is never angry.
The instruction is about the clock. Anger left overnight hardens into something else — an account of the other person that gets edited every time you retell it to yourself.
The rule does not require resolving everything before bed. It requires not going to sleep as enemies. Sometimes that is one sentence: I am still angry, and I am not leaving.
question: What are you currently carrying past sundown, some of it for years?
practice: Close one thing today with a message or a call, even if the issue is not solved.
prayer: Father, I have let anger sleep beside me. Take it before tonight.

title: When they are far away
text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
body: Many in this church are married across a distance, parenting across a distance, and grieving across a distance. The Preacher's warning is exactly about that: the danger is not the falling but the falling alone.

A video call is not nothing — it is the lifting up, done at range, and it should be defended in the diary like a shift. Distance kills a relationship by attrition, one skipped call at a time, not by any single decision.
It also means finding someone here. A marriage held together across an ocean still needs people in the room who will pick you up on a bad night.
question: Who would notice if you fell this month — here, in this country?
practice: Fix a standing time with the person at home, and tell one person here how you actually are.
prayer: God, hold the people I love while I cannot. Give me someone here who will lift me up.

title: The other family
text: In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor preferring one another;
body: The word Paul uses for affection is the one for family love — the bond between siblings. He is deliberately applying it to people who are not related.

That is the New Testament's answer to loneliness, and it is not a small one: the church is not a service you attend but a household you belong to, and it is meant to be inconvenient in the way families are.
In honour preferring one another means going first. Somebody has to, and the instruction is written to you rather than about them.
question: Are you a member of a household here, or an attender of a service?
practice: Invite one person from church to eat this week. Go first.
prayer: Lord, make this church a family to me, and make me a brother in it.
